problems.problem: For two given distinct points $A$ and $B$ of the plane, find the locus of points $C$ such that the triangle $ABC$ is acute-angled and its angle $A$ is the middle one in size.
Find $x_{1000}$ if $x_1=4$, $x_2=6$, and for every natural $n\geqslant 3$, $x_n$ is the smallest composite number greater than $2x_{n-1}-x_{n-2}$.

A paper triangle with angles $20^\circ$, $20^\circ$ and $140^\circ$ is cut along one of its angle bisectors into two triangles, one of which is again cut along an angle bisector, and so on. Can a triangle similar to the original one be obtained after several cuts?
Petya has exactly $28$ classmates. Any two of the $28$ have different numbers of friends in this class. How many friends does Petya have?
To every pair of numbers $x$ and $y$ some number $x*y$ is assigned. Find $1993*1935$ if it is known that for any three numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$ the identities $x*x=0$ and $x*(y*z)=(x*y)+z$ hold.
A convex quadrilateral $ABMC$ is given in which $AB=BC$, $\angle BAM=30^\circ$, $\angle ACM=150^\circ$. Prove that $AM$ is the bisector of the angle $BMC$.
Is there a non-convex pentagon no two of whose five diagonals have common points (other than vertices)?

Kolya has a segment of length $k$, and Lyova has a segment of length $l$. First Kolya divides his segment into three parts, and then Lyova divides his segment into three parts. If two triangles can be formed from the resulting six segments, Lyova wins, and if not, Kolya wins. Which of the players, depending on the ratio $k/l$, can secure a win, and how should he play?
Prove that the equation $x^2+y^2+z^2=x^3+y^3+z^3$ has infinitely many solutions in integers $x$, $y$, $z$.

Two circles intersect at the points $A$ and $B$. At the point $A$ tangents to both circles are drawn, meeting the circles at the points $M$ and $N$. The lines $BM$ and $BN$ meet the circles once more at the points $P$ and $Q$ ($P$ on the line $BM$, $Q$ on the line $BN$). Prove that the segments $MP$ and $NQ$ are equal.
Find the largest natural number not ending in zero which decreases by an integer factor when one of its digits (not the first) is deleted.
Prove that if any number of threes is inserted between the zeros of the number $12008$, the resulting number is divisible by $19$.

An equilateral triangle $ABC$ is given. For an arbitrary point $P$ inside the triangle, consider the points $A'$ and $C'$ in which the lines $AP$ and $CP$ meet $BC$ and $BA$ respectively. Find the locus of points $P$ for which the segments $AA'$ and $CC'$ are equal.
A rectangle of size $1\times k$, for any natural $k$, will be called a strip. For which natural $n$ can a $1995\times n$ rectangle be cut into pairwise different strips?
Natural numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ are such that $ab=cd$. Can the number $a+b+c+d$ be prime?

Initially four identical right triangles are given. At each move one of the existing triangles is cut along the altitude (issuing from the right angle) into two others. Prove that after any number of moves there will be two identical triangles among the triangles.
Prove that any convex polygon has at most $35$ angles smaller than $170^\circ$.
Prove that if the numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ satisfy the inequalities $|a-b|\geqslant|c|$, $|b-c|\geqslant|a|$, $|c-a|\geqslant|b|$, then one of these numbers equals the sum of the other two.

A circle is circumscribed about a triangle $ABC$, and tangents to it are drawn through the points $A$ and $B$; they meet at the point $M$. The point $N$ lies on the side $BC$, and the line $MN$ is parallel to the side $AC$. Prove that $AN=NC$.

The integers from $1$ to $n$ are written in a row. Under them the same numbers are written in a different order. Can it happen that the sum of each number and the number written under it is a perfect square a) for $n=9$; b) for $n=11$; c) for $n=1996$?
Let $A$ and $B$ be points lying on a circle. They divide the circle into two arcs. Find the locus of the midpoints of all chords whose endpoints lie on different arcs $AB$.

Ali Baba and a robber are dividing a treasure consisting of $100$ gold coins laid out in $10$ piles of $10$ coins. Ali Baba chooses $4$ piles, puts a mug next to each of them, and puts several coins into each mug (at least one, but not the whole pile). The robber must rearrange the mugs in some way, changing their original arrangement, after which the coins are poured from the mugs into the piles next to which the mugs now stand. Then Ali Baba again chooses $4$ piles out of $10$, puts mugs next to them, and so on. At any moment Ali Baba may leave, taking with him any three piles of his choice. The remaining coins go to the robber. What is the largest number of coins Ali Baba can take away if the robber also tries to get as many coins as possible?
In a triangle one side is $3$ times smaller than the sum of the other two. Prove that the angle opposite to it is the smallest angle of the triangle.

There are $9$ different pieces of cheese on a plate. Is it always possible to cut one of them into two parts so that the resulting $10$ pieces can be divided into two portions of equal mass with $5$ pieces in each?

In a convex hexagon $AC_1BA_1CB_1$ the sides are equal in pairs: $AB_1=AC_1$, $BC_1=BA_1$, $CA_1=CB_1$, and $\angle A+\angle B+\angle C=\angle A_1+\angle B_1+\angle C_1$. Prove that the area of the triangle $ABC$ equals half the area of the hexagon.

$N$ trains run around a circle in one direction at equal distances from each other. On this railway, at the vertices of an equilateral triangle, there are stations $A$, $B$, $C$ (labelled in the direction of motion). Ira enters station $A$ and at the same time Lyosha enters station $B$, in order to leave on the nearest trains.

It is known that if they enter the stations at the moment when the engine driver Roma is passing through the forest, then Ira will board a train earlier than Lyosha, and in all other cases Lyosha boards earlier than Ira or at the same time as her. What part of the railway passes through the forest?

$2n$ sportsmen held a round-robin tournament twice (in a round-robin tournament everybody meets everybody else; a win gives one point, a draw $1/2$, a loss $0$). The sum of points of each of them changed by at least $n$.

Prove that it changed by exactly $n$ for everybody.

Let $1+x+x^2+\ldots+x^{n-1}=F(x)G(x)$, where $F$ and $G$ are polynomials whose coefficients are zeros and ones ($n>1$). Prove that one of the polynomials $F(x)$, $G(x)$ can be represented in the form $(1+x+x^2+\cdots+x^{k-1})T(x)$, where $T$ is also a polynomial with coefficients $0$ and $1$, and $k>1$.
Is the number $4^9+6^{10}+3^{20}$ prime?

In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ the altitudes $AD$ and $CE$ are drawn. A square $ACPQ$ and rectangles $CDMN$ and $AEKL$ are constructed, with $AL=AB$, $CN=CB$. Prove that the area of the square $ACPQ$ equals the sum of the areas of the rectangles $AEKL$ and $CDMN$.

A traveller visited a village in which every person either always tells the truth or always lies. The inhabitants of the village stood in a circle, and each told the traveller about his neighbour on the right whether that person is truthful or a liar. On the basis of these statements the traveller determined uniquely what fraction of all the inhabitants of the village are truthful. Determine it yourself.

In the country of Nashiya there are military bases connected by roads. A set of roads is called important if, after these roads are closed, there are two bases not connected by a path. An important set is called strategic if it does not contain a smaller important set. Prove that the set of roads belonging to exactly one of two different strategic sets forms an important set.
A point $O$ lies inside a rhombus $ABCD$. The angle $DAB$ equals $110^\circ$. The angles $AOD$ and $BOC$ equal $80^\circ$ and $100^\circ$ respectively. What can the angle $AOB$ be equal to?

Several distinct points are marked on the segment $[0,1]$. Each marked point lies either exactly in the middle between two other marked points (not necessarily adjacent to it), or exactly in the middle between a marked point and an endpoint of the segment. Prove that all the marked points are rational.

Two numbers are written on the blackboard in a laboratory. Every day the senior researcher Petya erases both numbers and writes instead their arithmetic mean and their harmonic mean. On the morning of the first day the numbers $1$ and $2$ were written on the board. Find the product of the numbers written on the board in the evening of the $1999$-th day.

(The arithmetic mean of two numbers $a$ and $b$ is the number $\dfrac{a+b}{2}$, and the harmonic mean is the number $\dfrac{2}{\frac1a+\frac1b}$.)

Two players play the following game: the first writes in a row, as he wishes, letters A or B (from left to right, one after another; one letter per move), and after each move of the first player the second interchanges any two of the letters written or changes nothing (this also counts as a move). After both players have made $1999$ moves each, the game ends. Can the second player play so that, whatever the first player does, the result is a palindrome (that is, a word that reads the same from left to right and from right to left)?

The diagonals of a parallelogram $ABCD$ meet at the point $O$. The circle passing through the points $A$, $O$, $B$ touches the line $BC$. Prove that the circle passing through the points $B$, $O$, $C$ touches the line $CD$.

Find all positive integers $k$ such that the number
$$\underbrace{1\ldots1\overbrace{2\ldots2}^{k}}_{2000}-\underbrace{2\ldots2}_{1001}$$
is the square of an integer.

The incircle of a triangle $ABC$ ($AB>BC$) touches the sides $AB$ and $AC$ at the points $P$ and $Q$ respectively, $RS$ is the midline parallel to $AB$, and $T$ is the intersection point of the lines $PQ$ and $RS$. Prove that $T$ lies on the bisector of the angle $B$ of the triangle.

$2^n$ people take part in an $n$-event competition. For every sportsman his strength in each of the events of the programme is known. The competition is held as follows: first all the sportsmen take part in the first event, and the better half of them go on to the next round. This half takes part in the next event, and half of them go on to the next round, and so on, until the winner is determined in the $n$-th event. Call a sportsman a "possible winner" if the events can be arranged in the programme so that he becomes the winner.

a) Prove that it may happen that at least half of the sportsmen are "possible winners".

b) Prove that the number of "possible winners" never exceeds $2^n-n$.

c) Prove that it may happen that there are exactly $2^n-n$ "possible winners".

$23$ natural numbers (not necessarily distinct) are written in a row. Prove that brackets and signs of addition and multiplication can be placed between them so that the value of the resulting expression is divisible by $2000$.
A circle and a point $A$ inside it are given. Find the locus of the vertices $C$ of all possible rectangles $ABCD$ whose vertices $B$ and $D$ lie on the circle.

Grisha wrote the numbers $1, 2, 3, \ldots, 63, 64$ in the squares of a chessboard in some order. He told Lyosha only the sum of the numbers in each rectangle of two squares and added that $1$ and $64$ lie on one diagonal. Prove that from this information Lyosha can determine exactly which number is written in which square.

$ABCD$ is a convex quadrilateral. The circles constructed on the segments $AB$ and $CD$ as diameters touch each other externally at a point $M$ different from the intersection point of the diagonals of the quadrilateral. The circle passing through the points $A$, $M$ and $C$ meets for the second time the line joining the point $M$ and the midpoint of $AB$ at the point $K$, and the circle passing through the points $B$, $M$ and $D$ meets the same line for the second time at the point $L$. Prove that $|MK-ML|=|AB-CD|$.

A system of fortifications consists of dugouts. Some of the dugouts are connected by trenches, and from any dugout one can run to some other one. An infantryman is hiding in one of the dugouts. A cannon can cover any dugout with one shot. In each interval between shots the infantryman must run along one of the trenches to a neighbouring dugout (even if the cannon has just fired at the neighbouring dugout, the infantryman may run there). Call the system reliable if the cannon has no guaranteed strategy for hitting the infantryman (that is, a sequence of shots thanks to which the cannon hits the infantryman regardless of his initial location and subsequent movements).

a) Prove that the system of fortifications shown in the figure is reliable.

b) Find all reliable systems of fortifications that cease to be reliable after the destruction of any one of the trenches.

Can four footballers be placed on a football field so that the pairwise distances between them are $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$, $5$ and $6$ metres?

In a certain country the total salary of the $10\%$ best-paid workers makes up $90\%$ of the salary of all workers. Can it be that in each of the regions into which this country is divided, the salary of any $10\%$ of the workers makes up at most $11\%$ of the total salary paid in this region?

A point $A$ is marked inside an angle with vertex $M$. A ball was released from this point; it was reflected from one side of the angle at the point $B$, then from the other side at the point $C$, and returned to $A$ ("the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection", see the figure). Prove that the centre $O$ of the circle circumscribed about the triangle $BCM$ lies on the line $AM$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo9_2001_0_p3_fig.png

Stones lie in three piles: $51$ stones in one, $49$ stones in another, and $5$ stones in the third. It is allowed to merge any piles into one, and also to divide a pile with an even number of stones into two equal ones. Is it possible to obtain $105$ piles with one stone in each?
A natural number $N$ is $\underbrace{99\ldots9}_{k}$ times greater than the sum of its digits. Indicate all possible values of $k$ and for each of them give an example of such a number.

The participants of a chess tournament played one game with each other. For each participant $A$ the number of points he scored was counted (a win gives $1$ point, a draw $1/2$ point, a loss $0$ points), as well as his strength coefficient by the formula: the sum of the points of those participants whom $A$ beat, minus the sum of the points of those to whom he lost.

a) Can the strength coefficients of all the participants be greater than $0$?

b) Can the strength coefficients of all the participants be less than $0$?

A rank of recruits stood facing the sergeant. At the command "left turn" some of them turned to the left, some to the right, and the rest turned about. Can the sergeant always take a place in the rank so that there are equally many recruits facing him on both sides of him?
Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be the sides of a triangle. Prove the inequality $a^3+b^3+3abc>c^3$.

The bisectors of the angles $A$ and $C$ of a triangle $ABC$ meet its circumcircle at the points $E$ and $D$ respectively. The segment $DE$ meets the sides $AB$ and $BC$ at the points $F$ and $G$ respectively. Let $I$ be the intersection point of the bisectors of the triangle $ABC$. Prove that the quadrilateral $BFIG$ is a rhombus.
Find all integers $x$ and $y$ satisfying the equation $x^4-2y^2=1$.

$n$ light bulbs were arranged in a row and some of them were switched on. Every minute after that all the bulbs change state simultaneously: the bulbs that were on during the previous minute go out, and those that were off during the previous minute and were adjacent to exactly one lit bulb light up. For which $n$ can some bulbs be lit at the beginning so that afterwards at every moment there is at least one lit bulb?

An acute-angled triangle was cut by a straight cut into two parts (not necessarily triangular), then one of these parts again into two parts, and so on: at each step any one of the existing parts was chosen and cut (along a straight line) into two. After several steps it turned out that the original triangle had fallen apart into several triangles. Can all of them be obtuse-angled?

The hooligans Jay and Bob drew tadpoles at a technical drawing lesson (the four circles in the figure have the same radius, the triangle is equilateral, and the horizontal side of this triangle is a diameter of the circle). Which of the tadpoles has the larger area?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo9_2003_0_p1_fig.png
The product of five numbers is not zero. Each of these numbers was decreased by one, and their product did not change. Give an example of such numbers.

A shop has three floors, between which one can move only by lift. A study of the attendance of the floors of the shop showed that from the beginning of the working day until the shop closes:

— of the customers entering the lift on the second floor, half go to the first floor and half to the third;

— of the customers leaving the lift, fewer than a third do so on the third floor.

To which floor did customers travel more often from the first floor, the second or the third?

There is a chocolate bar in the form of an equilateral triangle with side $n$, divided by grooves into equilateral triangles with side $1$. Two players play. In one move one may break off a triangular piece of the bar along a groove, eat it, and pass the rest to the opponent. The player who receives the last piece, a triangle with side $1$, is the winner. A player who cannot make a move loses early. Who wins with correct play?

A right triangle $ABC$ with hypotenuse $AB$ is inscribed in a circle. Let $K$ be the midpoint of the arc $BC$ not containing the point $A$, $N$ the midpoint of the segment $AC$, and $M$ the intersection point of the ray $KN$ with the circle. Tangents to the circle are drawn at the points $A$ and $C$; they meet at the point $E$. Prove that $\angle EMK=90^\circ$.

$100$ prisoners were put in a prison. The warden told them: "I will give you an evening to talk with each other, then I will put you in separate cells, and you will not be able to communicate any more. From time to time I will take one of you to a room in which there is a lamp (initially it is switched off). When leaving the room, you may leave the lamp either on or off.

If at some moment one of you tells me that all of you have already been in the room, and is right, then I will set you all free. And if he is wrong, I will feed you all to the crocodiles. And do not worry that somebody will be forgotten: if you keep silent, all of you will visit the room, and for nobody will any visit to the room be the last one."

Devise a strategy guaranteeing the prisoners' release.
Every day at 12:00 the share price of the company "Horns and Hoofs" rises or falls by $17$ percent (the price is not rounded). Can the share price take the same value twice?

The coefficients $p$ and $q$ of the quadratic equation $x^2+px+q=0$ were increased by one. This operation was repeated nine times. Could it happen that each of the ten resulting equations has integer roots?

A billiard table has the form of a polygon (not necessarily convex) whose adjacent sides are perpendicular to each other. The vertices of this polygon are pockets; a ball falling into one stays there. A ball is released from a vertex with an (interior) angle of $90^\circ$ and is reflected from the cushions (the sides of the polygon) by the law "the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection". Prove that the ball will never return to this vertex.

Let $l_a$, $l_b$ and $l_c$ be the lengths of the bisectors of the angles $A$, $B$ and $C$ of a triangle $ABC$, and $m_a$, $m_b$ and $m_c$ the lengths of the corresponding medians. Prove that
$$\frac{l_a}{m_a}+\frac{l_b}{m_b}+\frac{l_c}{m_c}>1.$$

Call a natural number allowed if it has at most $20$ distinct prime divisors. Initially there is a pile of $2004!$ (that is, $1\cdot2\cdot\ldots\cdot2004$) stones. Two players in turn take from the pile some allowed number of stones (possibly a new one each time). The player who takes the last stones wins. Who wins with correct play?

A deck of $36$ cards lies face down in front of a psychic ($4$ suits, nine cards of each suit). He names the suit of the top card, after which the card is turned over and shown to him. After that the psychic names the suit of the next card, and so on. The psychic's task is to guess the suit as many times as possible.

The backs of the cards are asymmetric, and the psychic sees in which of two positions the top card lies. The psychic's assistant knows the order of the cards in the deck and cannot change it, but he can place the back of each card in one way or the other.

Could the psychic make an agreement with his assistant, while the latter did not yet know the order of the cards, ensuring that the suit is guessed for at least a) $19$ cards; b) $23$ cards?

If you have devised a way of guessing some other number of cards greater than $19$, write it down too.
The discriminants of three monic quadratic trinomials are $1$, $4$ and $9$. Prove that one can choose one root of each of them so that their sum equals the sum of the remaining roots.
Are there $2005$ distinct natural numbers such that the sum of any $2004$ of them is divisible by the remaining number?

A circle $\omega_1$ passes through the centre of a circle $\omega_2$. From a point $C$ lying on $\omega_1$, tangents to $\omega_2$ are drawn, meeting $\omega_1$ for the second time at the points $A$ and $B$. Prove that the segment $AB$ is perpendicular to the line passing through the centres of the circles.
Is it true that any triangle can be cut into $1000$ parts from which a square can be assembled?

$n$ digits, none of which is $0$, are written around a circle. Senya and Zhenya copy into their notebooks $n-1$ digits, reading them clockwise. It turned out that although they started from different places, the $(n-1)$-digit numbers they wrote down coincided. Prove that the circle can be cut into several arcs so that the digits written on the arcs form identical numbers.

An acute-angled triangle $ABC$ and a point $P$ not coinciding with the intersection point of its altitudes are given. Prove that the circles passing through the midpoints of the sides of the triangles $PAB$, $PAC$, $PBC$ and $ABC$, and also the circle passing through the projections of the point $P$ onto the sides of $\triangle ABC$, meet at one point.

For the 23rd of February Vasya was given $777$ sweets. Vasya wants to eat all the sweets in $n$ days, so that on each of these days (except the first, but including the last) he eats one sweet more than on the previous day. For what largest number $n$ is this possible?

At an olympiad $m>1$ schoolchildren solved $n>1$ problems. All the schoolchildren solved different numbers of problems. All the problems were solved by different numbers of schoolchildren. Prove that one of the schoolchildren solved exactly one problem.

An acute-angled triangle $ABC$ is given. On the sides $AB$ and $BC$, congruent rectangles $ABMN$ and $LBCK$ are constructed externally so that $AB=KC$. Prove that the lines $AL$, $NK$ and $MC$ meet at one point.
In the expression $(x^4+x^3-3x^2+x+2)^{2006}$ the brackets were expanded and like terms collected. Prove that the coefficient of some power of the variable $x$ is negative.

Call a path a closed trajectory in the plane consisting of arcs of circles and passing through each of its points exactly once. Give an example of a path and of a point $M$ on it such that every line passing through $M$ bisects the path, that is, the sum of the lengths of all pieces of the path in one half-plane equals the sum of the lengths of all pieces of the path in the other half-plane.

A teacher filled a $5\times 5$ table of cells with distinct integers and gave one copy of it each to Borya and Misha. Borya chooses the largest number in the table, then crosses out the row and the column containing this number, then chooses the largest of the remaining numbers, crosses out the row and the column containing this number, and so on. Misha performs similar operations, each time choosing the smallest numbers. Can the teacher fill the table so that the sum of the five numbers chosen by Misha is greater than the sum of the five numbers chosen by Borya?
The number of the present olympiad ($70$) is formed by the last digits of the year in which it is held, written in reverse order. How many more times will this situation occur in this millennium?

Four points $A$, $B$, $C$, $D$ are chosen on the parabola $y=x^2$ so that the lines $AB$ and $CD$ meet on the ordinate axis. Find the abscissa of the point $D$ if the abscissae of the points $A$, $B$ and $C$ are $a$, $b$ and $c$ respectively.
Find all increasing finite arithmetic progressions that consist of prime numbers and whose number of terms is greater than the common difference of the progression.

A convex figure $F$ has the following property: any equilateral triangle with side $1$ can be translated so that all its vertices fall on the boundary of $F$. Is $F$ necessarily a disc? (A figure is called convex if the segment joining any two of its points lies entirely inside the figure.)

$n>4$ teams played a single round-robin football tournament. A win gave $3$ points, a draw $1$, a loss $0$. It turned out that all the teams scored equal numbers of points.

a) Prove that there are $4$ teams having equal numbers of wins, equal numbers of draws and equal numbers of losses.

b) For what smallest $n$ may there be no $5$ such teams?

The sides of a triangle $ABC$ are seen from a point $T$ at angles of $120^\circ$. Prove that the lines symmetric to the lines $AT$, $BT$ and $CT$ with respect to the lines $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ respectively meet at one point.

Two KVN teams take part in a game of four contests. For each contest each of six judges gives a mark, an integer from $1$ to $5$; a computer finds the arithmetic mean of the marks for the contest and rounds it to tenths. The winner is determined by the sum of the four values obtained by the computer. Can it happen that the sum of all the marks given by the judges to the losing team is greater than that of the winning team?

A cyclist travels along a circular road, always moving in one direction. Every day he covers $71$ km and stops for the night at the roadside. On the road there is an anomalous zone of length $71$ km. If the cyclist stops for the night in it at a distance of $y$ km from one boundary of the zone, he wakes up at the opposite place of the zone, at a distance of $y$ km from its other boundary. Prove that, no matter where the cyclist began his journey, sooner or later he will stop for the night in that place.

Let $AL$ be the bisector of a triangle $ABC$, $O$ the centre of the circle circumscribed about this triangle, and $D$ the point on the side $AC$ such that $AD=AB$. Prove that the lines $AO$ and $LD$ are perpendicular.

Call a complication of a number the insertion of one digit into it at the beginning, at the end or between any two of its digits. Is there a natural number from which it is impossible to obtain a perfect square by means of a hundred complications?

Vasya has $100$ bank cards. Vasya knows that there is $1$ rouble on one of the cards, $2$ roubles on another, and so on, $100$ roubles on the last one, but he does not know how much money is on which card. Vasya can insert a card into a cash machine and request some sum. The machine pays out the requested sum if it is on the card, pays out nothing if there is not that much money on the card, and swallows the card in any case. The machine does not show how much money was on the card. What is the largest sum Vasya can be sure to get?
Show that there exists a convex figure bounded by arcs of circles that can be cut into several parts from which two convex figures bounded by arcs of circles can be assembled.
After a lesson the graph of the function $y=\dfrac kx$ and five lines parallel to the line $y=kx$ ($k\ne0$) remained on the board. Find the product of the abscissae of all ten intersection points.
Prove that there exists a polygon which can be divided by a segment into two congruent parts so that this segment bisects one of the sides of the polygon and divides another one in the ratio $2:1$.

In every cell of a $101\times 101$ square there is one of two signs: "turn" or "straight". A toy car can enter from outside into any cell on the boundary of the square (at right angles to the boundary). If the car gets into a cell with the sign "straight", it continues to move in the same direction as before. If it gets into a cell with the sign "turn", it turns through $90^\circ$ to either side, at its choice. A treasure is hidden in the central cell of the square. Can the signs be placed so that the car has no possibility of getting into the central cell?

Call a sequence of natural numbers interesting if each of its terms, except the first, is either the arithmetic mean or the geometric mean of the two terms adjacent to it. Senya began a sequence with three natural numbers forming an increasing geometric progression. He would like to continue his sequence to an infinite interesting sequence which from no moment on becomes either an arithmetic or a geometric progression. Can it turn out that this cannot be done?

(The arithmetic mean of two numbers $a$ and $b$ is the number $(a+b)/2$, and the geometric mean is the number $\sqrt{ab}$. A sequence of positive numbers each term of which, starting from the second, equals the arithmetic mean (the geometric mean) of the terms adjacent to it, is an arithmetic (geometric) progression.)

The angle $B$ at the vertex of an isosceles triangle $ABC$ equals $120^\circ$. From the vertex $B$ two rays at an angle of $60^\circ$ to each other were sent into the triangle; after being reflected from the base $AC$ at the points $P$ and $Q$, they hit the lateral sides at the points $M$ and $N$ (see the figure). Prove that the area of the triangle $PBQ$ equals the sum of the areas of the triangles $AMP$ and $CNQ$.

An integer $n>1$ is given. Two players in turn mark points on a circle: the first in red, the second in blue (one may not mark the same point twice). When $n$ points of each colour have been marked, the game ends. After that each player finds on the circle an arc of the greatest length with endpoints of his own colour on which there are no other marked points. The player whose arc found is longer wins (if the lengths of the arcs are equal, and also if neither player has such arcs, it is a draw). Can one of the players secure a win?

After eating three piglets and seven kids on an empty stomach, the Grey Wolf was still suffering from hunger. But another time he ate $7$ piglets and a kid on an empty stomach and suffered from overeating. What will the Wolf suffer from if he eats $11$ kids on an empty stomach?

A point $M$ is chosen on the side $AB$ of a rectangle $ABCD$. Through this point a perpendicular to the line $CM$ is drawn; it meets the side $AD$ at the point $E$. The point $P$ is the foot of the perpendicular dropped from the point $M$ to the line $CE$. Find the angle $APB$.

Every inhabitant of the town of Tmutarakan has his own cockroaches, not all the same number. Two cockroaches are called comrades if they have a common owner (in particular, every cockroach is its own comrade). Which is greater: the average number of cockroaches owned by an inhabitant of the town, or the average number of comrades of a cockroach?

$2009$ numbers are placed around a circle, each equal to $+1$ or $-1$, and not all the numbers are equal. Consider all possible groups of ten consecutive numbers. We find the product of the numbers in each group of ten and add them up. What is the largest sum that can be obtained?
An open non-self-intersecting broken line of $37$ segments is given. Through each segment a line was drawn. What is the smallest number of distinct lines that could have been obtained?

Tolya wants to obtain a one-digit number from a given natural number. To do this, he is allowed to place plus signs between the digits arbitrarily and compute the sum (for example, from the number $123456789$ one can obtain $12345+6+789=13140$). With the number obtained one is again allowed to perform a similar operation, and so on. Prove that a one-digit number can always be obtained in $10$ operations.

In a tournament each participant met each other participant once. Each game was refereed by one referee, and all the referees refereed different numbers of games. The player Ivanov claims that all his games were refereed by different referees. The players Petrov and Sidorov claim the same about themselves. Can it be that none of them is mistaken?

In a right triangle $ABC$ with right angle $C$, the angle $A$ equals $30^\circ$. The point $I$ is the centre of the inscribed circle of the triangle $ABC$, and $D$ is the intersection point of the segment $BI$ with this circle. Prove that the segments $AI$ and $CD$ are perpendicular.

Three natural numbers not exceeding $40$ are written on the board. In one move one may increase any of the written numbers by a number of percent equal to one of the two remaining numbers, if the result is an integer. Are there initial numbers such that in several moves one of the numbers on the board can be made greater than $2011$?

In a trapezoid $ABCD$ with bases $AD$ and $BC$ the rays $AB$ and $DC$ meet at the point $K$. The points $P$ and $Q$ are the centres of the circumcircles of the triangles $ABD$ and $BCD$. Prove that $\angle PKA=\angle QKD$.

$(n-1)n$ expressions are written on the board: $x_1-x_2$, $x_1-x_3$, $\ldots$, $x_1-x_n$, $x_2-x_1$, $x_2-x_3$, $\ldots$, $x_2-x_n$, $\ldots$, $x_n-x_{n-1}$, where $n\geqslant 3$. Lyosha wrote in his notebook all these expressions, their sums of two distinct ones, of three distinct ones, and so on, up to the sum of all the expressions. In all the sums he wrote down, Lyosha collected like terms (for example, instead of $(x_1-x_2)+(x_2-x_3)$ Lyosha writes $x_1-x_3$, and instead of $(x_1-x_2)+(x_2-x_1)$ he writes $0$). How many expressions did Lyosha write in his notebook exactly once?

In the country of Dalyokaya a province is called large if more than $7\%$ of the inhabitants of the country live in it. It is known that for every large province there are two provinces with smaller populations whose total population is greater than that of this large province. What is the smallest number of provinces the country of Dalyokaya can have?

$2n$ pears lie in a row. The masses of any two neighbouring pears differ by at most $1$ g. Prove that all the pears can be put into $n$ bags with two pears in each and these bags laid out in a row so that the masses of any two neighbouring bags also differ by at most $1$ g.

In a parallelogram $ABCD$ the perpendicular $BH$ to the side $AD$ is dropped. A point $M$ equidistant from the points $C$ and $D$ is marked on the segment $BH$. Let the point $K$ be the midpoint of the side $AB$. Prove that the angle $MKD$ is a right angle.
Rational numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$ are such that all the numbers $x+y^2+z^2$, $x^2+y+z^2$ and $x^2+y^2+z$ are integers. Is it true that the number $2x$ is an integer?

A triangle $ABC$ is given. A line $l$ touches its incircle. Denote by $l_a$, $l_b$, $l_c$ the lines symmetric to $l$ with respect to the bisectors of the exterior angles of the triangle. Prove that the triangle formed by these lines is congruent to the triangle $ABC$.

a) $75$ teams took part in a football tournament. Each team played each other team once; for a win in a match a team received $3$ points, for a draw $1$ point, for a loss $0$ points. It is known that any two teams scored different numbers of points. Find the smallest possible difference between the points of the teams that took the first and the last places.

b) The same question for $n$ teams.

Pies lie at equal intervals around a round table. Igor walks around the table and eats every third pie he meets (each pie may be met several times). When no pies were left on the table, he noticed that the last pie he took was the first one he had met, and that he had walked exactly $7$ circles around the table. How many pies were there?

In a triangle $ABC$, where the angle $B$ is right and the angle $A$ is smaller than the angle $C$, the median $BM$ is drawn. A point $L$ is taken on the side $AC$ so that $\angle ABM=\angle MBL$. The circumcircle of the triangle $BML$ meets the side $AB$ at the point $N$. Prove that $AN=BL$.

It is known about positive numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, $e$ that
$$a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2+e^2=ab+ac+ad+ae+bc+bd+be+cd+ce+de.$$
Prove that among these numbers there are three for which no triangle with such side lengths exists.

Cut the figure shown in the picture into two congruent parts.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo9_2013_0_p4_fig.png

Call a point of the plane a node if both its coordinates are integers. A triangle with vertices at nodes is given, and at least two nodes lie inside it. Prove that among the nodes inside the triangle one can choose two such that the line through them contains one of the vertices of the triangle or is parallel to one of the sides of the triangle.

A hundred sages want to travel by a suburban train of $12$ carriages from the first to the $76$-th station. They know that at the first station two inspectors will board two carriages of the train. After the fourth station, on each stretch between stations one of the inspectors will move to an adjacent carriage, and they take turns. A sage sees an inspector only if he is in the adjacent carriage or one carriage away. At each station each sage may run along the platform at most three carriages (for example, from the $7$-th carriage a sage can run to any carriage with number from $4$ to $10$ and get into it). What is the largest number of sages who can avoid ever being in the same carriage as an inspector, no matter how the inspectors move? (The sages receive no information about the inspectors other than that given in the problem. The sages agree on a strategy in advance.)
All the coefficients of a quadratic trinomial are odd integers. Prove that it has no roots of the form $1/n$, where $n$ is a natural number.

$21$ white and $21$ purple shirts hang in a row in a shop. Find the smallest $k$ such that for any initial order of the shirts one can take down $k$ white and $k$ purple shirts so that the remaining white shirts hang consecutively and the remaining purple shirts also hang consecutively.
$n$ sticks are given. From any three of them an obtuse-angled triangle can be formed. What is the largest possible value of $n$?

A square tablecloth lies on a square table so that no corner of the table is covered, but a triangular piece of the tablecloth hangs down from each side of the table. It is known that some two adjacent pieces are congruent. Prove that the other two pieces are also congruent. (The tablecloth nowhere overlaps itself; its dimensions may differ from those of the table.)

The radical of a natural number $N$ (denoted $\operatorname{rad}(N)$) is the product of all the prime divisors of $N$, each taken once. For example, $\operatorname{rad}(120)=2\cdot3\cdot5=30$.

Is there a triple of pairwise coprime natural numbers $A$, $B$, $C$ such that $A+B=C$ and $C>1000\cdot\operatorname{rad}(ABC)$?

$10$ points are marked on a circle, numbered clockwise $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_{10}$, and it is known that they can be divided into pairs of points symmetric with respect to the centre of the circle.

Initially a grasshopper sits at each marked point. Every minute one of the grasshoppers jumps along the circle over its neighbour so that the distance between them does not change. It is not allowed to fly over other grasshoppers or to land at a point where a grasshopper already sits.

After some time it turned out that some $9$ grasshoppers sit at the points $A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_9$, and the tenth grasshopper sits on the arc $A_9A_{10}A_1$. Can one assert that it sits exactly at the point $A_{10}$?
Is there a natural number $n$ such that the numbers $n$, $n^2$, $n^3$ begin with the same digit, different from one?

All the natural numbers from $1$ to $1000$ are placed around a circle in some order so that each of the numbers is a divisor of the sum of its two neighbours. It is known that the number $k$ has two odd neighbours. What parity can the number $k$ have?

Every day Frau Bock bakes a square $3\times 3$ cake. Carlson immediately cuts out for himself four square $1\times 1$ pieces with sides parallel to the sides of the cake (not necessarily along the lines of the $3\times 3$ grid). After that the Kid cuts out for himself from the remaining part of the cake a square piece with sides also parallel to the sides of the cake. What is the largest piece of cake the Kid can count on regardless of Carlson's actions?

The points $O$ and $I$ are the centres of the circumscribed and inscribed circles of a scalene triangle $ABC$. Two equal circles touch the sides $AB$, $BC$ and $AC$, $BC$ respectively; besides, they touch each other at the point $K$. It turned out that $K$ lies on the line $OI$. Find $\angle BAC$.

The emperor invited $2015$ wizards to a festival, some of whom are good and the rest evil. A good wizard always tells the truth, while an evil one may say anything. The wizards know who is good and who is evil, but the emperor does not.

At the festival the emperor asks each wizard (in the order he wishes) one question that can be answered "yes" or "no". Having questioned all the wizards, the emperor expels one of them. The expelled wizard goes out through an enchanted door, and the emperor learns whether he was good or evil. Then the emperor again asks each of the remaining wizards one question, again expels one, and so on, until the emperor decides to stop (he may do this after any question).

Prove that the emperor can expel all the evil wizards, removing at most one good one in the process.

Are there two polynomials with integer coefficients such that each of them has a coefficient whose absolute value is greater than $2015$, while all the coefficients of the product of these two polynomials have absolute values not exceeding $1$?
The sum of three positive numbers equals their product. Prove that at least two of them are greater than one.
In a triangle $ABC$ a point $K$ is marked on the extension of the median $CM$ beyond the point $C$ so that $AM=CK$. It is known that the angle $BMC$ equals $60^\circ$. Prove that $AC=BK$.

Vasya was given as homework the equation $x^2+p_1x+q_1=0$, where $p_1$ and $q_1$ are integers. He found its roots $p_2$ and $q_2$ and wrote down the new equation $x^2+p_2x+q_2=0$. Having repeated the operation three more times, Vasya noticed that he had solved $4$ quadratic equations and all of them had integer roots (if exactly one of the two possible equations had roots, Vasya always chose it, and if both did, either one). However, no matter how hard Vasya tried, he could not form a fifth equation having real roots, and Vasya was very upset. What equation was Vasya given as homework?

The point $O$ is the centre of the circumcircle of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$. A line perpendicular to the side $AC$ meets the segment $BC$ and the line $AB$ at the points $Q$ and $P$ respectively. Prove that the points $B$, $O$ and the midpoints of the segments $AP$ and $CQ$ lie on one circle.
Is there a $2016$-digit number from which, by permuting its digits, one can obtain $2016$ different $2016$-digit perfect squares?

In the country of linguists there are $n$ languages. $m$ people live there, each of whom knows exactly $3$ languages, and for different people these sets are different. It is known that the largest number of people any two of whom can talk without an interpreter equals $k$. It turned out that $11n\leqslant k\leqslant \dfrac m2$. Prove that then there are in the country at least $mn$ pairs of people who cannot talk without an interpreter.
Find the largest natural number all of whose decimal digits are distinct and which decreases $5$ times if its first digit is crossed out.

In a chess tournament each participant met each other participant once. In each round each participant played one game. In at least half of all the games both participants were fellow-countrymen (from the same city). Prove that in each round there was at least one game between fellow-countrymen.

Is there a polygon made of grid cells that can be divided into two congruent parts by a cut of the following shape (see the figure)? The cut must lie inside the polygon (only the ends of the cut may lie on the boundary).

a) the shape on the left; b) the shape on the right.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo9_2017_0_p3_fig.png
Find all pairs of natural numbers $a$ and $k$ such that for every natural number $n$ coprime to $a$ the number $a^{k^n+1}-1$ is divisible by $n$.

Petya coloured each cell of a $1000\times 1000$ square in one of $10$ colours. He also devised a $10$-cell polygon $\Phi$ such that for any way of cutting out of this square, along the cell boundaries, a polygon congruent to $\Phi$, all $10$ of its cells are of different colours. Must $\Phi$ be a rectangle?

In a triangle $ABC$ with angle $A$ equal to $45^\circ$ the median $AM$ is drawn. The line $b$ is symmetric to the line $AM$ with respect to the altitude $BB_1$, and the line $c$ is symmetric to the line $AM$ with respect to the altitude $CC_1$. The lines $b$ and $c$ meet at the point $X$. Prove that $AX=BC$.
$81$ non-zero numbers are written in a row. The sum of any two neighbouring numbers is positive, and the sum of all the numbers is negative. What can the sign of the product of all the numbers be?
Four sticks are given. It turned out that from any three of them a triangle can be formed, and the areas of all four triangles are equal. Must all the sticks be of the same length?

Prove that for any natural numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_k$ such that $\frac1{a_1}+\frac1{a_2}+\cdots+\frac1{a_k}>1$, the equation $\left[\frac n{a_1}\right]+\left[\frac n{a_2}\right]+\cdots+\left[\frac n{a_k}\right]=n$ has at most $a_1a_2\ldots a_k$ solutions in natural numbers. ($[x]$ is the integer part of the number $x$, that is, the largest integer not exceeding $x$.)

A convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ with pairwise non-parallel sides is given. An arbitrary point $P$ different from $A$ and $D$ is chosen on the side $AD$. The circumcircles of the triangles $ABP$ and $CDP$ meet for the second time at the point $Q$. Prove that the line $PQ$ passes through a fixed point independent of the choice of the point $P$.

Call an arrangement of $n$ ones and $m$ zeros around a circle good if one can interchange a neighbouring zero and one in it so that an arrangement differing from the original one by a rotation is obtained. For which natural $n$, $m$ does a good arrangement exist?

$2018$ participants came to an olympiad; some of the participants are acquainted with each other. We say that several pairwise acquainted participants form a "circle" if every other participant of the olympiad is not acquainted with someone of them. Prove that all the participants of the olympiad can be seated in $90$ classrooms so that no classroom contains all the members of any "circle".

A king summoned two sages and announced a task to them: the first one thinks of $7$ distinct natural numbers with sum $100$, secretly tells them to the king, and names to the second sage only the fourth largest of these numbers, after which the second one must guess the numbers thought of. The sages have no opportunity to confer. Can the sages be sure to cope with the task?
Find the smallest natural number $n$ for which $n^2+20n+19$ is divisible by $2019$.

In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ the altitudes $AA'$ and $BB'$ are drawn. The point $O$ is the centre of the circle circumscribed about the triangle $ABC$. Prove that the distance from the point $A'$ to the line $BO$ equals the distance from the point $B'$ to the line $AO$.

Each segment with endpoints at vertices of a regular $100$-gon was coloured red if there is an even number of vertices between its endpoints, and blue otherwise (in particular, all the sides of the $100$-gon are red). Numbers were placed at the vertices whose sum of squares equals $1$, and on the segments the products of the numbers at their endpoints. Then the sum of the numbers on the blue segments was subtracted from the sum of the numbers on the red segments. What is the largest number that could be obtained?

The bisector of the angle $ABC$ meets the circumcircle $\omega$ of the triangle $ABC$ at the points $B$ and $L$. The point $M$ is the midpoint of the segment $AC$. On the arc $ABC$ of the circle $\omega$ a point $E$ is chosen such that $EM\parallel BL$. The lines $AB$ and $BC$ meet the line $EL$ at the points $P$ and $Q$ respectively. Prove that $PE=EQ$.

There are $100$ piles of $400$ stones each. In one move Petya chooses two piles, removes one stone from each of them, and gets for this as many points as the absolute value of the difference of the numbers of stones in these two piles now. Petya must remove all the stones. What is the largest total number of points he can get?
Is there a natural number divisible by $2020$ in which all the digits $0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9$ occur equally often?

Two triangles (three sticks in each) are formed from six sticks of pairwise different lengths. Is it always possible to form from them one triangle whose sides consist of one, two and three sticks respectively?

Three bogatyrs are fighting the dragon Zmei Gorynych. Ilya Muromets with each of his blows cuts off half of all the heads and one more, Dobrynya Nikitich a third of all the heads and two more, and Alyosha Popovich a quarter of all the heads and three more. The bogatyrs strike one at a time, in the order they consider necessary. If none of the bogatyrs can strike because the number of heads would become non-integer, the Dragon eats the bogatyrs. Will the bogatyrs be able to cut off all the heads of a $20^{20}$-headed Dragon?

In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ ($AB<BC$) the altitude $BH$ is drawn. The point $P$ is symmetric to the point $H$ with respect to the line joining the midpoints of the sides $AC$ and $BC$. Prove that the line $BP$ contains the centre of the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$.

$3n$ guests came to Ivan's birthday party. Ivan has $3n$ top hats with the letters A, B and C written on top, $n$ of each type. Ivan wants to arrange a ball: to put the top hats on the guests and line them up in round dances (one or more) so that the length of each round dance is divisible by $3$, and, looking at any round dance from above, one reads clockwise ABCABC$\ldots$ABC. Prove that Ivan can arrange the ball in exactly $(3n)!$ different ways. (Top hats with the same letters are indistinguishable; all the guests are different.)

Gleb thought of natural numbers $N$ and $a$, $a<N$. He wrote the number $a$ on the board. Then he began to perform the following operation: divide $N$ with remainder by the last number written on the board, and write the remainder obtained on the board as well. When the number $0$ appeared on the board, he stopped. Could Gleb have chosen initially $N$ and $a$ such that the sum of the numbers written was greater than $100N$?
Positive numbers $a$ and $b$ are such that $a-b=a/b$. Which is greater, $a+b$ or $ab$?

The cells of a paper $8\times 8$ square are coloured in two colours. Prove that Arseny can cut out of it along the grid lines two $2\times 2$ squares without common cells whose colourings coincide. (Colourings differing by a rotation are considered different.)

$30$ light bulbs are placed at the nodes of the grid of a $4\times 5$ squared rectangle; initially all of them are off. In one move one may draw any line not touching the bulbs (the sizes of the bulbs are to be neglected, regarding them as points) such that on some one side of it no bulb is lit, and switch on all the bulbs on that side of the line. Each move must switch on at least one bulb. Can all the bulbs be switched on in exactly four moves?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo9_2021_0_p3_fig.png

The point $M$ is the midpoint of the side $BC$ of a triangle $ABC$. A circle $\omega$ passes through the point $A$, touches the line $BC$ at the point $M$, and meets the side $AB$ at the point $D$ and the side $AC$ at the point $E$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the midpoints of the segments $BE$ and $CD$ respectively. Prove that the circle circumscribed about the triangle $MXY$ touches $\omega$.

$100N$ sandwiches, each with sausage and cheese, lie in a row. Uncle Fyodor and the cat Matroskin play a game. In one action Uncle Fyodor eats one sandwich from one of the ends. In one action the cat Matroskin may pull the sausage off one sandwich (or may do nothing). On each move Uncle Fyodor makes $100$ actions in a row, while the cat Matroskin makes only $1$ action; Uncle Fyodor moves first, the cat Matroskin second, and then the moves alternate until Uncle Fyodor has eaten all the sandwiches. Uncle Fyodor wins if the last sandwich he ate was with sausage. Is it true that for every natural $N$ he can win regardless of the cat Matroskin's moves?

Let $p$ and $q$ be coprime natural numbers. A frog jumps along the number line, starting at the point $0$, each time either by $p$ to the right or by $q$ to the left. Once the frog returned to $0$. Prove that for every natural $d<p+q$ there are two numbers visited by the frog that differ by $d$.

For each of the nine natural numbers $n, 2n, 3n, \ldots, 9n$ the first digit from the left was written down. Can there be, for some natural $n$, at most four distinct digits among the nine digits written down?

Rectangles $ABCD$ and $DEFG$ are placed so that the point $D$ lies on the segment $BF$, and the points $B$, $C$, $E$, $F$ lie on one circle (see the figure). Prove that $\angle ACE=\angle CEG$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo9_2022_0_p2_fig.png

Sasha's collection consists of coins and stickers; there are fewer coins than stickers, but there is at least one coin. Sasha chose some positive number $t>1$ (not necessarily an integer). If he increases the number of coins $t$ times without changing the number of stickers, his collection will contain $100$ items. If instead he increases the number of stickers $t$ times without changing the number of coins, he will have $101$ items. How many stickers could Sasha have had? Find all possible answers and prove that there are no others.

Some cells of a $100\times 100$ board are coloured black. In all the rows and columns that contain black cells their number is odd. In each row containing black cells we put a red counter on the middle black cell (by count). In each column containing black cells we put a blue counter on the middle black cell (by count). It turned out that all the red counters are in different columns and the blue counters in different rows. Prove that there is a cell containing both a blue and a red counter.

Two triangles intersect in a hexagon which cuts off $6$ small triangles from them. The radii of the incircles of these six triangles are equal. Prove that the radii of the incircles of the two original triangles are also equal.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/mmo9_2022_0_p5_fig.png

A convex polygon $M$ and a prime number $p$ are given. It turned out that there are exactly $p$ ways to divide $M$ into equilateral triangles with side $1$ and squares with side $1$. Prove that the length of one of the sides of the polygon $M$ equals $p-1$.

Sasha writes the numbers $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ in some order, puts the signs of arithmetic operations "$+$", "$-$", "$\times$" and brackets, and looks at the value of the resulting expression. For example, he can obtain the number $8$ by the expression $(4-3)\times(2+5)+1$. Can he obtain the number $123$?

Forming numbers out of several others is not allowed (for example, the number $12$ cannot be formed from the numbers $1$ and $2$).

Two sequences of the letters A and B are given, each containing $100$ letters. In one operation one may insert at some place of a sequence (possibly at the beginning or at the end) one or several identical letters, or remove from the sequence one or several consecutive identical letters. Prove that the second sequence can be obtained from the first in at most $100$ operations.

The perimeter of a triangle $ABC$ equals $1$. A circle $\omega$ touches the side $BC$, the extension of the side $AB$ at the point $P$ and the extension of the side $AC$ at the point $Q$. The line passing through the midpoints of $AB$ and $AC$ meets the circumcircle of the triangle $APQ$ at the points $X$ and $Y$. Find the length of the segment $XY$.

A natural number $n>1$ is given. Call a positive common fraction (not necessarily irreducible) good if the sum of its numerator and denominator equals $n$. Prove that every positive common fraction whose denominator is less than $n$ can be expressed in terms of good fractions (not necessarily distinct) by means of the operations of addition and subtraction if and only if $n$ is a prime number.

Recall that a common fraction is the ratio of an integer to a natural number.
A regular $100$-gon was cut into several parallelograms and two triangles. Prove that these triangles are congruent.

Call a triple of numbers a triplet if one of them equals the arithmetic mean of the other two. The sequence $(a_n)$ is constructed as follows: $a_0=0$, $a_1=1$, and for $n>1$ the number $a_n$ is the smallest natural number greater than $a_{n-1}$ such that among the numbers $a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_n$ there are no three forming a triplet. Prove that $a_{2023}\leqslant 100\,000$.

Real numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ are such that
$$\frac ab+\frac ba=\frac cd+\frac dc.$$
Prove that the product of some two of the numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$ equals the product of the other two.

$12$ children, all of different strength, came to a physical education lesson. The teacher divided them $10$ times into two teams of $6$ people, each time in a new way, and held a tug-of-war contest. Could it happen that all $10$ times the contest ended in a draw (that is, the sums of the strengths of the children in the teams were equal)?

Petya thought of a positive irreducible fraction $x=\frac mn$. In one move Vasya names a positive irreducible fraction $y$ not exceeding $1$, and Petya tells Vasya in reply the numerator of the irreducible fraction equal to the sum $x+y$. How can Vasya find $x$ for certain in two moves?

On the circumcircle of a triangle $ABC$ the midpoints of the arcs $BAC$ and $CBA$, the points $M$ and $N$ respectively, and the midpoints of the arcs $BC$ and $AC$, the points $P$ and $Q$ respectively, are marked. A circle $\omega_1$ touches the side $BC$ at the point $A_1$ and the extensions of the sides $AC$ and $AB$. A circle $\omega_2$ touches the side $AC$ at the point $B_1$ and the extensions of the sides $BA$ and $BC$. It turned out that $A_1$ lies on the segment $NP$. Prove that $B_1$ lies on the segment $MQ$.

$9$ vertical posts stand in a row. At some places between neighbouring posts horizontal sticks are inserted, no two of which are at the same height. A beetle crawls from bottom to top; when it meets a stick, it crawls along it to the neighbouring post and continues to crawl upwards. It is known that if the beetle starts at the bottom of the first post, it finishes its way on the ninth post. Is it always possible to remove one of the sticks so that the beetle, starting at the bottom of the first post, ends up at the top of the fifth post?

For example, if the sticks are arranged as in the figure, the beetle will crawl along the solid line. If the third stick on the beetle's path is removed, it will crawl along the dashed line.

A real number is written on each of $99$ cards. All $99$ numbers are distinct, and their total sum is irrational. A stack of the $99$ cards is called unlucky if for every natural $k$ from $1$ to $99$ the sum of the numbers on the top $k$ cards is irrational. Petya computed in how many ways the original cards can be put into an unlucky stack. What is the smallest value he could have obtained?
Can nine distinct integers be placed in the cells of a $3\times 3$ table so that the product of the numbers in each row equals $2025$ and the product of the numbers in each column also equals $2025$?

Can an infinite number of chess knights be placed on the infinite squared plane (at most one knight per cell) so that each knight attacks exactly $6$ others?

In a triangle $ABC$ with right angle $C$ the altitude $CH$ is drawn. A circle passing through the points $C$ and $H$ meets the segments $AC$, $CB$ and $BH$ for the second time at the points $Q$, $P$ and $R$ respectively. The segments $HP$ and $CR$ meet at the point $T$. Which is greater: the area of the triangle $CPT$ or the sum of the areas of the triangles $CQH$ and $HTR$?

Each cell of a $100\times 100$ square is coloured either white or black. It turned out that each white cell has exactly two side-adjacent cells coloured white, and each black cell has exactly two side-adjacent cells coloured black. Find the largest possible number of black cells.

A housewife has a piece of meat with which she wants to feed three cats. Every few seconds the housewife cuts off a bit of meat and feeds it to one of the cats of her choice, and each bit must be one and the same fraction of the piece from which it is cut. After some time the housewife puts the rest of the meat into the refrigerator. Can she feed the cats equal amounts of meat?

The altitudes $AA_1$, $BB_1$, $CC_1$ of an acute-angled triangle $ABC$ meet at the point $H$. The bisector of the angle $CBH$ meets the segment $CH$ at the point $X$, and the bisector of the angle $BCH$ meets the segment $BH$ at the point $Y$. Denote the angle $XA_1Y$ by $\alpha$. Define $\beta$ and $\gamma$ similarly. Find the value of the sum $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$.

Alice wrote down positive numbers $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, $e$ (not necessarily integers), and Marusya the numbers $\frac1a$, $\frac1b$, $\frac1c$, $\frac1d$, $\frac1e$. It turned out that the sum of Alice's numbers is greater than the sum of Marusya's numbers. Could the product of Alice's numbers be smaller than the product of Marusya's numbers?

An acute-angled triangle $ABC$ is given. On its circumcircle the point $D$ diametrically opposite to the vertex $A$ is marked. Points $X$ and $Y$ on the side $BC$ are such that $BX=XD$ and $CY=YD$ (the point $X$ lies on the segment $BY$). Prove that $DA$ is the bisector of the angle $XDY$.

$11$ watermelons with masses $1, 2, 3, \ldots, 11$ kg lie on a table. Alyona and Bogdan put the watermelons into four bags; each bag withstands $14$ kg and tears under a greater weight. They take turns choosing a watermelon from the table and putting it into any of the bags so that the bag does not tear. The player who cannot make a move loses. Alyona begins. Who can secure a win no matter how the other plays?

In a convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ the sides $AB$ and $BC$ are equal, and $K$ is the intersection point of the diagonals. The circumcircle of the triangle $ABD$ meets the side $BC$ for the second time at the point $Y$, and the circumcircle of the triangle $BCD$ meets the side $AB$ for the second time at the point $X$. Prove that $\angle AKX=\angle CKY$.

Is there an infinite set $S$ consisting of squares of natural numbers such that for any two distinct $x$ and $y$ from $S$ there is $z$ from $S$ (possibly coinciding with $x$ or $y$) for which $x+y+z$ is the square of a natural number?

A hotel has $a>1$ floors, with $b$ single rooms on each floor. $ab$ mathematicians arrived at a mathematical congress. It turned out that each mathematician likes exactly one room on each floor. Prove that the number of ways to accommodate all the mathematicians in the hotel so that each likes his room is even.
